_meta.description: Plainly's local glossary. Each entry maps a technical term to plain-English explanations. 'simple' is required; everything else is optional.

fields.why: why this matters to the user
fields.next: a gentle suggested next step, if one makes sense
fields.aliases: other spellings/phrases that mean the same thing
fields.category: grouping for filtering and future expansion
fields.risk: low | medium | high — how careful the user should be
fields.replaceable: false = never substituted inline by Replace Mode (name-like terms); tooltips, the side panel, and glosses still explain them. Default true.

repository.detailed: The main home for your files, updates, and project history. Everything about one project lives here.
repository.why: Almost everything on GitHub happens inside a repository.

commit.simple: save this version with a note
commit.detailed: A saved snapshot of your project at one moment in time, with a short note describing what changed.
commit.why: Commits let you go back to any earlier version if something breaks.

pull request.detailed: A polite, reviewable request to merge your changes into the main project. Others can look it over before anything changes.
pull request.why: Nothing in the main project changes until someone approves it.
pull request.next: If you're ready to share your changes, open a pull request and describe what you did in plain words.

fork.detailed: Your own personal copy of someone else's project that you can change freely without affecting the original.
fork.why: You can experiment safely — the original project is never touched.

branch.simple: a safe testing version of your project
branch.detailed: A safe copy of your project where you can test changes without affecting the main version.
branch.why: If your experiment doesn't work out, the main version stays untouched.

merge.detailed: Taking changes from one version of the project and folding them into another, usually into the main version.
merge.why: Merging is how approved work becomes part of the real project.

clone.simple: download a full copy to your computer
clone.detailed: Downloading a complete copy of a project — files and history — onto your own computer so you can work on it.

push.detailed: Sending the versions you saved on your computer up to the online project so others (and your tools) can see them.

pull.detailed: Fetching the newest changes from the online project down to your computer so you're up to date.

deploy.detailed: Taking your project from 'files in a folder' to 'a real website or app people can visit'.
deploy.why: Until you deploy, your changes exist but nobody on the internet can see them.
deploy.next: When you're happy with your changes, look for a Deploy or Publish button.

build.simple: prepare your project to go live
build.detailed: The automatic process that packages your files into their final, publishable form. It happens before a site goes live.

build failed.simple: the site/app could not finish preparing
build failed.detailed: Something stopped your project from being packaged for publishing. Your live site is usually unaffected — the previous version stays up.
build failed.why: Your newest changes are not live yet, but nothing is broken for visitors.
build failed.next: Open the build log and look at the first error message — it usually names the file causing trouble.

production.simple: the real, live version people see
production.detailed: The version of your site or app that the public actually uses — as opposed to test versions only you can see.
production.why: Changes to production affect real visitors immediately.

staging.simple: a private practice version of your site
staging.detailed: A private copy of your site used to check changes before showing them to the public.

preview deployment.simple: a temporary test version of your site
preview deployment.detailed: A temporary, shareable version of your site created so you can check changes before they go live for everyone.

domain.detailed: The name people type to reach your site, like yoursite.com.

dns.detailed: The system that connects your website's name (like yoursite.com) to the computer that actually hosts it. DNS changes can take a few hours to spread.

ssl certificate.simple: the padlock that makes your site secure
ssl certificate.detailed: A digital certificate that encrypts traffic to your site and gives visitors the padlock icon. Most platforms set this up automatically.

environment variable.simple: a private setting your app reads
environment variable.detailed: A named value (often a password or key) stored outside your code so your app can use it without exposing it publicly.
environment variable.why: Keys stored this way stay out of your public code.

api.simple: a way for apps to talk to each other
api.detailed: A set of rules that lets one piece of software ask another for information or actions — like a waiter carrying requests between you and the kitchen.

api key.simple: a password that lets an app use a service
api key.detailed: A secret code that proves your app is allowed to use a service. Treat it like a password — never share it publicly.
api key.why: Anyone who has your key can use the service as you, sometimes spending your money.
api key.next: If a key may have leaked, regenerate it from the service's dashboard.

webhook.simple: an automatic message sent when something happens
webhook.detailed: A way for one service to instantly notify another when an event occurs — like a doorbell between two apps.

oauth.simple: log in using another account you already have
oauth.detailed: A safe way to let one app access another account (like 'Sign in with Google') without giving away your password.

authentication.detailed: The process of confirming you are who you say you are, usually with a password, code, or linked account.

two-factor authentication.simple: a second check when you log in
two-factor authentication.detailed: An extra login step (like a code from your phone) that keeps your account safe even if someone learns your password.

readme.detailed: The first document people see in a project. It explains what the project is and how to use it.

markdown.detailed: A lightweight way to format text using symbols — like *stars* for bold — that gets turned into styled text.

open source.simple: free for anyone to use and improve
open source.detailed: Software whose code is public — anyone can read it, use it, and suggest improvements.

license.simple: the rules for using this project
license.detailed: A document stating what others are allowed to do with the project — use it, change it, sell it, and so on.

dependency.simple: other code your project needs to work
dependency.detailed: A piece of ready-made code your project borrows so you don't have to build everything from scratch.

ci/cd.detailed: Robots that automatically test your changes and publish them when everything passes — so you don't have to do it by hand.

issue.simple: a tracked task, bug, or idea
issue.detailed: A note attached to a project describing a bug, request, or task, so work can be discussed and tracked in one place.

rollback.simple: go back to an earlier working version
rollback.detailed: Undoing a recent change by switching back to a version that worked before.
rollback.why: This is your safety net — most mistakes can be undone with a rollback.

cache.simple: saved copies that make things faster
cache.detailed: Temporarily stored copies of files so pages load faster. Sometimes you see old content until the cache clears.

cdn.simple: a network that delivers your site quickly worldwide
cdn.detailed: A group of servers around the world that hold copies of your site so it loads fast for everyone, everywhere.

serverless.simple: code that runs without you managing a server
serverless.detailed: A way to run small pieces of code in the cloud only when needed — the platform handles all the machinery for you.

localhost.simple: your own computer, acting as a private test site
localhost.detailed: A version of your site running only on your computer. Nobody else on the internet can see it.

terminal.simple: the text window for typing commands
terminal.detailed: A window where you control your computer by typing commands instead of clicking buttons.

json.simple: a structured format computers use to share data
json.detailed: A simple text format for organizing information — labels and values — that both humans and computers can read.

sandbox.detailed: A protected test environment where you can try things without affecting anything real — common in payment tools like Stripe.

rate limit.simple: a cap on how often you can ask
rate limit.detailed: A limit on how many requests you can make in a period of time. Hitting it means 'slow down', not 'something is broken'.

zap.simple: an automated recipe connecting two apps
zap.detailed: In Zapier, a Zap is an automation: when something happens in one app, it triggers an action in another.

trigger.simple: the event that starts an automation
trigger.detailed: The 'when this happens' part of an automation — like 'when a new email arrives'.

payload.detailed: The package of information one app sends to another in a request or notification.

latency.simple: how long things take to respond
latency.detailed: The delay between asking for something and getting it. Lower is faster.

uptime.simple: how often your site is working
uptime.detailed: The percentage of time your site is online and reachable. 99.9% uptime means almost never down.

instance.simple: one running copy of an app or server
instance.detailed: A single running copy of a program or server. More instances usually means handling more visitors.

framework.simple: a ready-made foundation for building apps
framework.detailed: A pre-built structure (like Next.js or React) that handles common work so builders can focus on what makes their project unique.

migration.simple: a structured change to stored data
migration.detailed: A controlled update to how data is stored — like reorganizing a filing cabinet without losing any files.
